---
title: The short form, service()
description: A whole integration in about ten lines, with every field explained.
sidebar: { order: 2 }
---

Most integrations are the same thing: call an endpoint or two, show some numbers. Say that, and `service()` does the rest.

```js title="data/integrations/speedbox.mjs"
export default ({ service, fmt }) => service({
  type: 'speedbox',
  name: 'Speedbox',
  icon: 'wifi',
  auth: { header: 'X-Api-Key' },
  get: { latest: '/api/results/latest' },
  stats: d => [
    { label: 'Down', value: d.latest.down, unit: ' Mbps' },
    { label: 'Up', value: d.latest.up, unit: ' Mbps' },
    { label: 'Ping', value: d.latest.ping, unit: ' ms' },
    { label: 'Last run', value: fmt.day(d.latest.at) },
  ],
  sample: { latest: { down: 940, up: 41, ping: 11, at: '2026-10-29T08:00:00Z' } },
  expect: { Down: 940, Up: 41, Ping: 11 },
});
```

That file is a whole integration. From it you get:

- The config: `url`, `href`, `every`, `insecure`, and the credentials `auth` asks for. All checked, with unknown keys refused.
- Sign-in, including sessions and retries.
- A widget called `status`, with a tile for the small sizes.
- A read tool for the assistant, called `speedbox_status`.
- A failure message that never includes the key.

```yaml title="config.yaml"
integrations:
  speed:
    type: speedbox
    url: http://speedbox:8080
    key: ${SPEEDBOX_KEY}
layout:
  - widgets: [speed.status]
```

## Fields

| Field | Required | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | yes | The `type:` in `config.yaml`. |
| `name` | yes | The card's title. |
| `icon` | | The card's icon, by name. `pulse` by default. |
| `logo` | | The app's own icon, by dashboard-icons name. The `type` by default. |
| `auth` | | How it signs in. See [below](#auth). `none` by default. |
| `authOptional` | | Many installs run without a login: send credentials only if they're set. |
| `options` | | Settings of its own, as zod fields, beyond the URL and credentials. |
| `every` | | How often: seconds, or `5m`. A minute by default. Use it for heavy calls. |
| `get` | yes | Each call to make, by name. A map, or a function of the options. |
| `then` | | A second step that uses the first's answers. |
| `stats` | | Numbers: `{ label, value, unit, sub, tone, pct, trend }`. |
| `list` | | Rows. Used when there's no `stats`. |
| `status` | | Up or down items. The tile counts them. |
| `card` | | Anything the three above can't say. Return any [card](/cards/). |
| `headline` | | The tile. The first stat otherwise. |
| `about` | | What the assistant is told it's for, in a sentence. |
| `recap` | | [Slides](/build/recap/) for the year in review. |
| `sample` | yes | An answer per `get`, as the real service sends it. |
| `sampleOptions` | | Options to use with the sample. |
| `loginSample` | | What signing in answers, for a `login` that reads it. |
| `expect` | | Label to expected value. The check asks for it. |

`stats` wins if you give both it and `list`. With `status`, the card is a status card, and it says "2 down" or "9 up" by itself. A list says "Nothing here" when it's empty.

Numbers in `stats` are formatted for you: `1200` shows as `1,200`. A value that's undefined shows as `–`, and the check flags it.

## get

The keys you pick here become the keys of `d` in `stats`, and of `sample`.

```js
get: {
  stats: '/api/stats',                                      // a plain path
  jobs: { path: '/api/jobs', method: 'POST', body: { all: true } },
  version: { path: '/version', as: 'text', optional: true },
},
```

An entry can be a path, or an object with:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `path` | Added to the configured `url`. |
| `method` | `POST`. GET otherwise. |
| `body` | An object goes as JSON. A string or `URLSearchParams` goes as it is. |
| `headers` | Extra headers. |
| `as` | `text` for a plain answer, `headers` for the response's headers. |
| `optional` | If it fails, that key is undefined and the card still draws. |

Everything else must succeed, or the widget shows the error.

`get` can be a function of the options, and it also receives `session`, the sign-in token, for services that want it in a body.

```js
options: { org: z.string() },
get: o => ({ sites: `/v1/org/${o.org}/sites` }),
```

`then` runs after the first calls, and gets their answers:

```js
get: { nodes: '/api/nodes' },
then: d => ({ first: `/api/nodes/${d.nodes[0].id}` }),
```

## auth

| `auth` | What the config needs | What's sent |
|---|---|---|
| `'none'` | | Nothing. |
| `'bearer'` | `key` | `Authorization: Bearer <key>` |
| `'token'` | `key` | `Authorization: Token <key>` |
| `'basic'` | `username`, `password` | Basic auth. |
| `{ header: 'X-Api-Key', prefix: '' }` | `key` | That header. `prefix` is optional. |
| `{ query: 'apikey' }` | `key` | In the URL. The check makes sure errors don't show it. |
| `{ login: '/api/login', ... }` | `username`, `password` | Trades them for a session. |
| `{ handshake: { status: 409, header: 'X-Session-Id' } }` | optional `username`, `password` | A refused first request hands out a session id, sent back on the next. Transmission does this. |

A `login` can take more:

| Field | What it does |
|---|---|
| `login` | The path to post to. |
| `body` | `c => ({ ... })`: what to send. JSON, unless it's `URLSearchParams`. Username and password by default. |
| `token` | `r => r.jwt`: reads the token from the answer. Without it, Valet uses the session cookie. |
| `use` | `t => ({ 'X-Auth': t })`: how it's sent back. `Authorization: Bearer` by default. |
| `text` | The answer is plain text, not JSON. |
| `expired` | `a => a.error === 'auth'`: for services that say "signed out" with a 200. |
| `needs` | What it asks for: `username`, `password`, `key`. |
| `redirects` | The cookie comes on a redirect, so don't follow it. |
| `ttl` | Seconds a token lasts, for services that don't say. |

A `401` or `403` resets the session and tries once more.

## A status card

```js title="data/integrations/racks.mjs"
export default ({ service }) => service({
  type: 'racks',
  name: 'Racks',
  icon: 'cpu',
  auth: 'bearer',
  get: { nodes: '/api/nodes' },
  status: d => d.nodes.map(n => ({ name: n.name, ok: n.online, detail: n.online ? undefined : 'offline' })),
  sample: { nodes: [{ name: 'nas', online: true }, { name: 'pi', online: false }] },
  expect: { nas: true, pi: false },
});
```

## A login and a list

```js title="data/integrations/shelfy.mjs"
export default ({ service, z }) => service({
  type: 'shelfy',
  name: 'Shelfy',
  icon: 'book',
  auth: { login: '/api/login', token: r => r.jwt },
  options: { limit: z.number().int().default(5) },
  every: '5m',
  get: { books: '/api/books?sort=recent' },
  list: (d, o) => d.books.slice(0, o.limit).map(b => ({ title: b.title, subtitle: b.author })),
  sample: { books: [{ title: 'A Slow Winter', author: 'Sam Okafor' }, { title: 'Salt Road', author: 'Alex Lind' }] },
  loginSample: { jwt: 'tok' },
  expect: { 'A Slow Winter': 'Sam Okafor', 'Salt Road': 'Alex Lind' },
});
```

`expect` finds each row by its label, name or title, and compares its `value`, `meta`, `subtitle` or `ok`, in that order.

## Self-signed certificates

`insecure: true` in the config accepts a self-signed certificate, for that service only. Every `service()` takes it.

## Writing the sample

Paste a real answer, then remove anything personal. `sample` is what the tests use forever. `npm test` runs every built-in against its own, and `check-integration` does the same for yours.

A sample can't prove the service still answers that way. It proves your code reads that answer. If you have the real service, `npm run test:services` checks against it.

## When it isn't enough

For several widgets, buttons, or tools that change things, use the [full form](/build/full/). You can start from a template:

```sh
docker exec valet node dist/server.js new-integration my-service --full
```
